questions.topic: Language Standards — Nested Functions in ISO C
questions.q: Are nested functions supported by official C standards (C89, C99, C11, C17, C23)?
questions.hint: Think about whether the C standard allows declaring the body of one function inside the body of another.
options: No, according to the C standard all functions must be declared strictly at the global level
Yes, starting from the C99 standard
Yes, in all C standards without restrictions
Yes, but only if the nested function returns void
explanations: Correct! No official ISO C standard supports nested functions. All functions in standard C must be at the top level (file scope).
Incorrect. The C99 standard added compound literals and // comments, but not nested functions.
Incorrect. Standard C has never supported nested functions.
Incorrect. The return type has no effect on the standard prohibition.

questions.topic: Compiler Extensions — Support in GCC
questions.q: Which popular compiler provides support for nested functions as its own language extension (GNU C Extension)?
questions.hint: This compiler is often used in the Linux world and contains many non-standard C extensions.
options: GCC (GNU Compiler Collection)
MSVC (Microsoft Visual C++)
Standard C89 compiler
SDCC (Small Device C Compiler) in strict mode
explanations: Correct! GCC supports nested functions as a GNU C language extension. Other compilers (MSVC, Clang) in standard mode do not support this feature.
Incorrect. MSVC strictly enforces the absence of nested functions in C.
Incorrect. Nested functions are absent in the C89 standard.
Incorrect. Strict mode of compilers disables such extensions.

questions.topic: GCC Extensions — Accessing Variables of Outer Function
questions.q: What will the program output when compiled with the GCC compiler?
questions.hint: Does a nested function in GCC have access to local variables of its containing function?
options: Compilation error
explanations: Correct! A nested function in GCC has access to the lexical environment (lexical scope) and can read and modify local variables of the outer function. The value of $x$ will become $5 + 10 = 15$.
Incorrect. The nested function modified the value of $x$, not just read it.
Incorrect. The call `add_to_x(10)` managed to add to the initial value of 5.
Incorrect. In GCC compiler, this code will compile correctly.

questions.topic: Lifetime and Pointers — Danger of Calling via Pointer
questions.q: What consequence will calling `fn()` in main lead to if function `get_nested()` returns a pointer to its nested function?
questions.hint: What happens to the stack frame of function get_nested() after it completes its execution?
options: Undefined Behavior or Crash
The program will print the number 42 correctly and without errors
Compilation error at build stage
Function memory will automatically move to Heap
explanations: Correct! A nested function accesses the local variable `secret` residing on the stack of `get_nested()`. When `get_nested()` completes, its stack frame is destroyed. Calling via pointer afterwards leads to a crash or reading garbage (Dangling Pointer / Undefined Behavior).
Incorrect. Variable `secret` no longer exists on the stack.
Incorrect. Syntactically GCC will allow obtaining a pointer to a nested function, so the error will manifest at runtime.
Incorrect. Automatic transfer of stack variables to heap does not happen in C.

questions.topic: Security and Architecture — Trampolines and Executable Stack
questions.q: Why is generating pointers to nested functions in GCC considered a Security Risk?
questions.hint: How does GCC pass the context of a parent function to a nested function when called through a regular pointer?
options: GCC generates a small fragment of executable code ('trampoline') right on the stack, which requires an executable stack and violates NX/DEP protection
Nested functions clog the operating system import table
Pointers to nested functions always occupy more than 1024 bytes in memory
They lead to automatic decryption of private keys
explanations: Correct! To pass the context of the parent function, GCC dynamically creates a adapter instruction ('trampoline') on the stack. For this, the stack must have execution permissions (Executable Stack), which disables hardware NX/DEP protection and creates a vulnerability for Buffer Overflow attacks.
Incorrect. Nested functions are not related to OS import table.
Incorrect. A function pointer has a standard size (e.g., 8 bytes on 64-bit systems).
Incorrect. This is a distorted view of security issues.

questions.topic: GCC Syntax — Forward Declaration
questions.q: Which keyword in GCC extension allows making a forward declaration of a nested function before its full definition?
questions.hint: This keyword in regular C is used to automatically define the storage class of local variables.
options: auto
static
extern
inline
typedef
explanations: Correct! In GCC, forward declaration of a nested function is done using the keyword `auto`, for example: `auto void nested_func(int);`.
Incorrect. `static` sets internal linkage for global entities.
Incorrect. `extern` informs the compiler about declaring a function in another file/module.
Incorrect. `inline` is used for code inlining.
Incorrect. `typedef` creates a data type alias.

questions.topic: Clang/Apple Extensions — Blocks
questions.q: Which technology/extension in Clang/Apple compilers serves as an alternative to nested functions and uses syntax with the caret symbol `^`?
questions.hint: Pay attention to the declaration syntax of type `int (^my_block)(int)`.
options: Blocks (Blocks / Apple Blocks)
Nested Lambdas
Compound Functions
C99 Macros
explanations: Correct! Clang and Apple C use the 'Blocks' extension (`^`), which adds support for closures with the ability to copy context to the heap (`Block_copy`).
Incorrect. The term 'lambdas' is used in C++, C#, and other languages, but in Clang C it is called Blocks.
Incorrect. Compound applies to literals, not functions.
Incorrect. This is a full-fledged compiler syntax extension, not a macro preprocessor.

questions.topic: Scope — Scope of Nested Function Name
questions.q: What is the Scope of a nested function name declared inside function `process()`?
questions.hint: Is the nested function name visible outside the function in which it was created?
options: Name is limited only to code block / body of process() function
Name becomes available throughout the entire .c file
Name is accessible from any other project files (External Linkage)
Name is available only inside switch statements
explanations: Correct! A nested function has local scope (Block Scope) and is visible only inside the function (or `{}` block) where it was declared.
Incorrect. The name does not leak into global file scope.
Incorrect. Nested functions do not have external linkage.
Incorrect. Scope is limited to the declaration block, not just switch.

questions.topic: Comparing C and C++ — Closures and Lambda Expressions
questions.q: True or False: Unlike standard C, C++ (starting from C++11 standard) officially supports anonymous nested functions — Lambda Expressions?
questions.hint: Recall the capture-list syntax in C++: [=]() { ... }
options: True
False
explanations: Correct! C++11 added official support for lambda expressions (anonymous nested functions with context capture). Standard C still lacks this feature.
Incorrect. Lambdas are indeed a standardized part of C++11 and subsequent C++ versions.

questions.topic: Scope — Variable Shadowing
questions.q: What will the program output when executed?
questions.hint: How does local variable shadowing affect a variable in the outer context?
options: Compilation error
explanations: Correct! Declaration `int val = 100` inside `inner()` creates a new local variable that shadows outer `val`. The first print will output `100`, and after exiting `inner()`, outer `val` remains equal to `50`.
Incorrect. The variable inside `inner()` shadowed outer `val` and printed 100.
Incorrect. Outer `val` was not changed inside `inner()` because it was shadowed.
Incorrect. Redeclaring a variable in an inner block is syntactically allowed.

questions.topic: Nested Statements — Behavior of break inside switch in a Loop
questions.q: What will happen when executing a break statement inside a switch that is nested within a for loop?
questions.hint: Does break terminate both switch and the outer loop simultaneously?
options: The break statement terminates only the switch execution, while the loop will continue to the next iteration
The break statement terminates both switch and the outer for loop
A compilation error will occur due to context ambiguity
The program will loop infinitely
explanations: Correct! In C, `break` terminates only the innermost `switch` or loop in which it is directly contained. The outer `for` loop will continue executing.
Incorrect. Exiting the outer loop would require another `break`, an exit flag, or `goto`/`return`.
Incorrect. This is standard syntactic behavior in C.
Incorrect. The loop will complete all its iterations.

questions.topic: Control Flow — Early Return from Nested Loops
questions.q: What main advantage does using a return statement provide when searching for an element in a multidimensional array inside a function?
questions.hint: How many loops can a single break statement terminate compared to return?
options: return instantly terminates the function and exits all loop nesting levels simultaneously
return works faster because it does not use the stack
break cannot be used in nested loops at all
return guarantees automatic zeroing of the array
explanations: Correct! A single `break` statement exits only the innermost loop, requiring additional checks to exit remaining loops. A `return` statement immediately stops function execution regardless of loop nesting depth.
Incorrect. The advantage lies in control flow logic, not in abstract stack speed.
Incorrect. `break` can be used at any nesting level.
Incorrect. `return` does not affect array contents.

questions.topic: Branching — Dangling else Problem
questions.q: To which if statement does the else branch belong in the provided code when curly braces are omitted?
questions.hint: Recall the else binding rule in nested branches.
options: To the nearest preceding if that does not have its own else (to the inner if (b > 0))
To the first outer if (a > 0)
Compilation error — curly braces are required when nesting if statements
The else branch is ignored by the compiler
explanations: Correct! In C, the rule is: `else` is always attached to the *nearest* preceding `if` that does not have its own `else` (in this case, to `if (b > 0)`). Curly braces `{}` are needed to change this order.
Incorrect. Without braces, `else` never attaches to an outer `if` when an inner one is present.
Incorrect. Braces are recommended for readability, but syntax permits omitting them.
Incorrect. The `else` branch will compile normally.

questions.topic: Scope — Variable Shadowing in Nested Braces {}
questions.q: What will printf("%d", x) output at the end of function execution?
questions.hint: What value does variable x have in the scope where printf is called?
options: Compilation error
explanations: Correct! The innermost block with `x = 30` ends, and its `x` is destroyed. At `printf` level, variable `x = 20` declared in the `for` loop block is visible. Outer `x = 10` is still shadowed.
Incorrect. Variable with value 30 existed only inside the deepest `{}` block.
Incorrect. Variable `x = 10` is covered by variable `x = 20` from the loop block.
Incorrect. Declaring same-named variables in inner blocks is completely valid.

questions.topic: goto Statement — Exiting Deeply Nested Constructs
questions.q: In which situations is using the goto statement inside C functions considered accepted and justified practice (for example, in the Linux kernel)?
questions.hint: Think about error handling in functions that allocate multiple resources sequentially.
options: For centralized exit from deeply nested loops/conditions to a single resource cleanup block on errors
For replacing all while and for loops for optimization purposes
For transferring control from one function into the middle of another function
For automatic heap memory allocation
explanations: Correct! The `goto cleanup;` pattern is widely used in C system programming. It avoids duplicating resource release code (free, fclose) when exiting deeply nested checks.
Incorrect. Using `goto` instead of standard loops degrades readability and provides no benefits.
Incorrect. `goto` can only jump within a *single* function.
Incorrect. `goto` does not manage dynamic memory.

questions.topic: Nested Loops — continue Statement
questions.q: What will the program output when executing nested loops with a continue statement?
questions.hint: Which iteration and of which specific loop does continue skip?
explanations: Correct! When `j == 0`, `continue` triggers. It skips the rest of the *inner* loop `j` body and advances to `j++`. As a result, only pairs where `j == 1` are printed: `01` and `11`.
Incorrect. When `j == 0`, `printf` call is skipped, so `00` and `10` are not printed.
Incorrect. Iteration with `j == 0` is skipped, not `j == 1`.
Incorrect. Outer loop `i` will make two iterations (i=0 and i=1).

questions.topic: Switch Statements — Fallthrough in switch inside a Loop
questions.q: What will the code snippet output due to the absence of a break statement in case 0?
questions.hint: Trace the execution of case 0 and fallthrough into case 1.
options: ABB
AB
AB B
B
explanations: Correct! On iteration `i = 0`: hits `case 0` (prints `A`), then falls through into `case 1` (prints `B`) where `break` triggers. On iteration `i = 1`: hits `case 1` (prints `B`) where `break` triggers. Total: `ABB`.
Incorrect. On second iteration with `i = 1`, another letter `B` is printed.
Incorrect. There are no spaces in the output.
Incorrect. On first iteration both `case 0` and `case 1` execute.

questions.topic: switch Syntax — Declaring and Initializing Variables Before First case
questions.q: What will happen if you declare and initialize variable int a = 5; right after switch(...) {, but BEFORE the first case?
questions.hint: Will control pass to the initialization line when jumping via case label?
options: Variable will be declared in switch scope, but its initialization a = 5 will be skipped (a contains garbage)
Code will successfully initialize a = 5 on each entry to switch
Compilation error will occur
Variable a will become static
explanations: Correct! `switch` jumps (like `goto`) directly to the matching `case` label, skipping any initialization statements at the start of the block. Memory is allocated on stack, but value of `a` remains uninitialized.
Incorrect. The initialization line is physically bypassed when jumping to `case`.
Incorrect. In C this is syntactically allowed (unlike C++, where it would cause an error).
Incorrect. The `static` qualifier is not automatically added.

questions.topic: Infinite Loops — Exiting Nested while(1) via return
questions.q: What will calling function process(3) return?
questions.hint: Will the inner condition be able to stop both infinite loops?
options: Program will hang in an infinite loop
Runtime error
explanations: Correct! Despite two nested infinite loops `while(1)`, statement `return count;` triggers when `count` reaches 3, immediately returning control from function with value 3.
Incorrect. The `return` statement instantly breaks both loops.
Incorrect. Function will return value of variable `count`, which is 3.
Incorrect. Code is completely valid.

questions.topic: C99 Standard — Declaring Counters in Nested for Loops
questions.q: Will code compile in C99 standard and what will it output when redeclaring for (int i = 0; ...)?
questions.hint: Does a for loop counter have its own scope in C99?
options: Code compiles successfully and outputs: 0 1 0 1
Compilation error — redeclaration of variable i in the same function
Code outputs: 0 0 1 1
Loop becomes infinite
explanations: Correct! Starting from C99, variable declared in `for (int i...)` header has scope limited to that loop. Inner `i` shadows outer `i`, so code compiles and outputs `0 1 0 1 `.
Incorrect. Inner loop creates its own separate scope, so there is no error.
Incorrect. On each step of outer loop, inner loop runs fully from 0 to 1.
Incorrect. Inner loop does not corrupt counter value of outer loop.

questions.topic: Passing Parameters — Copying Base Types (Pass-by-Value)
questions.q: What will happen to variable `num` in `main` after executing function `add_five(num)`?
questions.hint: Does function modify a local variable copy or original?
options: Value of num will remain equal to 10
Value of num will become equal to 15
Compilation error will occur
Value of num will become equal to 0
explanations: Correct! In C, arguments are passed by value. Function `add_five` receives a copy of variable `num`, so increment `a += 5` occurs only inside local function context. In `main`, variable remains equal to 10.
Incorrect. That would happen only if pointer `&num` were passed.
Incorrect. Code is written without syntax errors.
Incorrect. Value of `num` in `main` is not reset.

questions.topic: Passing Arrays — Absence of Element Copying
questions.q: Is an array passed to a function with full copying of all its elements when declared `void process(int arr[])`?
questions.hint: What does array name turn into when passed as function parameter?
options: No, array is passed as a pointer to its first element, so element modifications are visible in calling function
Yes, C always fully copies entire array onto stack
explanations: Correct! When passing an array to a function, type decay occurs (Array Decay) — only address of its first element (`int *`) is passed. Copying of entire array does not happen, and element modifications inside function are visible outside.
Incorrect. In C, arrays are never automatically copied when passed to functions.

questions.topic: Argument Evaluation Order — Undefined Behavior (UB)
questions.q: What effect will calling `print_two(x++, x++)` lead to?
questions.hint: Is argument evaluation order specified in C standard (left-to-right or right-to-left)?
options: Undefined Behavior — argument evaluation order and sequence points between them are not specified in C
Guaranteed to output '5 6'
Guaranteed to output '6 5'
Compilation error — passing increment operators in arguments is forbidden
explanations: Correct! The C standard does not specify evaluation order of function arguments. Modifying same variable `x` multiple times without an intervening sequence point leads to Undefined Behavior.
Incorrect. Evaluation order is not guaranteed to be left-to-right.
Incorrect. Right-to-left evaluation order is also not guaranteed by standard.
Incorrect. Increment expressions are syntactically allowed in parameters, but create UB.

questions.topic: Passing Structures — Field Copying (Pass-by-Value)
questions.q: What happens when passing a structure by value to function `void process(struct Point p)`?
questions.hint: Unlike arrays, do structures behave like base types when passed?
options: A full copy of all structure fields is created on stack; any field modifications inside function will not affect original
Only a pointer to structure is passed, so original fields will change
Compilation error — structures in C are forbidden to pass without asterisk (*)
Only first 8 bytes of structure are passed
Structure is automatically saved to file
explanations: Correct! Unlike arrays, structures in C are passed by value entirely. Compiler copies contents of all structure fields onto stack.
Incorrect. For pointer passing, declaration must be `struct Point *p`.
Incorrect. Passing structures by value is fully supported by C language.
Incorrect. Entire structure is copied completely, regardless of its size.
Incorrect. Parameter passing is not related to I/O operations.

questions.topic: Multidimensional Arrays — Mandatory Specification of Dimensions
questions.q: Why when declaring function `void print_matrix(int m[][4], int rows)` is specifying dimension `[4]` for second dimension mandatory?
questions.hint: How does compiler calculate address of element $m[i][j]$ in one-dimensional RAM?
options: So compiler can correctly calculate element address using memory offset formula
This is a preprocessor requirement for memory allocation
Dimension `[4]` indicates total number of elements in matrix
This is optional — brackets `[][]` can be left empty
explanations: Correct! A 2D array is stored in memory as a continuous sequence of elements. To find address of element $m[i][j]$, compiler uses formula: $\text{base\_address} + (i \times \text{cols} + j) \times \text{sizeof(type)}$. Without knowing number of columns (`cols = 4`), compiling indexed access is impossible.
Incorrect. Address calculation is performed by compiler itself, not preprocessor.
Incorrect. Number 4 indicates only number of columns in one row.
Incorrect. Omitting all dimensions for multidimensional arrays will cause compilation error.

questions.topic: const Qualifier — Protecting Data via Pointer
questions.q: Which parameter declaration guarantees that function cannot modify the *value* pointed to by this pointer?
questions.hint: On which side of asterisk must const be located to protect addressed data?
options: const int *ptr
int * const ptr
int *ptr
void *ptr
explanations: Correct! Entry `const int *ptr` (or `int const *ptr`) means value of type `int` located at address `ptr` is read-only.
Incorrect. Entry `int * const ptr` creates a constant pointer: address itself cannot change, but modifying value at address `*ptr = ...` is allowed.
Incorrect. Regular pointer `int *ptr` permits modifying data at address.
Incorrect. `void *ptr` is simply an untyped pointer.

questions.topic: String Literals — Immutable Memory
questions.q: What consequence will calling function `zero_first("hello")` lead to?
questions.hint: In which memory region (.rodata) are string literals enclosed in double quotes placed?
options: Runtime error (Segmentation fault) — string literals are located in read-only memory
First character of string successfully replaced with null byte '\0'
Compilation error — cannot pass string literal into char* parameter
String 'hello' will become empty throughout entire program
Automatic heap memory allocation will occur
explanations: Correct! String literal `"hello"` is placed by compiler in write-protected memory section (`.rodata`). Attempting to write `s[0] = '\0'` will trigger a Segmentation Fault signal on most OS.
Incorrect. String literal memory is protected at OS level.
Incorrect. Under C standards passing literal into `char*` compiles (though in C++ it is forbidden or causes warning).
Incorrect. Change will not execute because program crashes on call.
Incorrect. Dynamic memory allocation does not occur.

questions.topic: Function Pointers — Implicit Conversion of Function Name
questions.q: True or False: When passing a function name as an argument (e.g., `apply(my_func)`), function name automatically converts to a pointer to it?
questions.hint: Is writing address-of operator `apply(&my_func)` strictly required?
options: True
False
explanations: Correct! Like arrays, function name in expressions and arguments automatically decays into a pointer to that function. Entries `apply(my_func)` and `apply(&my_func)` are completely equivalent.
Incorrect. In C, `&` operator before function name when passed in arguments is optional.

questions.topic: main Arguments — Type of argv Array
questions.q: What data type does parameter `argv` have in signature `int main(int argc, char *argv[])`?
questions.hint: An array of strings in C is represented as an array of pointers to char.
options: Array of pointers to character strings (char **)
Single character array (char *)
Pointer to array of integers (int *)
Array of structs struct Argument
File descriptor
explanations: Correct! Parameter `char *argv[]` converts to pointer to pointer `char **argv`, that is an array where each element contains address of null-terminated argument string.
Incorrect. `char *` represents only one string, whereas `argv` contains multiple arguments.
Incorrect. Command-line arguments are always passed as text (strings).
Incorrect. In C arguments are passed as array of strings, not structures.
Incorrect. File descriptors are integers for working with I/O.

questions.topic: Passing Optimization — const Struct * Instead of Copying
questions.q: Why when working with large structures is it recommended to pass parameter as `const StructType *s` instead of passing by value `StructType s`?
questions.hint: Think about byte count copied to stack on each call.
options: Only pointer (8 bytes) is passed, preventing expensive copying of entire structure onto stack, while const protects against changes
C forbids passing structures larger than 16 bytes by value
Passing by value automatically deletes structure from memory
This is the only way to pass structures with floating points
explanations: Correct! Passing structure by value copies each of its bytes onto stack. For large structures this reduces performance. Passing `const StructType *` copies only address (8 bytes on 64-bit systems), preserving data immutability via `const`.
Incorrect. C language allows passing structures of any size by value.
Incorrect. Passing by value creates local copy, but does not delete original.
Incorrect. Floating-point fields copy perfectly when passed by value.

questions.topic: Pointers to Pointers — Modifying Address Inside Function
questions.q: For a function to modify address stored in pointer itself (e.g., allocate dynamic memory for it), its parameter must accept:
questions.hint: Think what level of indirection is needed to modify variable of type int*.
options: Pointer to pointer (int **ptr)
Regular pointer (int *ptr)
Value of int type
Array int arr[]
explanations: Correct! To modify value of variable of type `int*` (write new address into it), you need to pass pointer to this variable into function, that is `int **ptr`.
Incorrect. Regular pointer `int *ptr` is passed by value (copied), and changing address inside function will not reflect in main.
Incorrect. Type `int` stores an integer, not a pointer.
Incorrect. Array `int arr[]` converts to `int *`, which does not allow modifying original pointer.

questions.topic: C99 Standard — static Keyword in Array Parameter Sizes
questions.q: What does entry `int arr[static 5]` mean in function parameter starting from C99 standard?
questions.hint: This is a hint to compiler about minimum guaranteed element count.
options: Argument is guaranteed to be a pointer to an array containing at least 5 elements
Array preserves its elements between function calls in static memory
Function will cause compilation error — such syntax is forbidden
Passed array must contain exactly 5 elements, passing larger size is forbidden
explanations: Correct! Construct `static N` in array parameter declaration provides guarantee to compiler that passed pointer is non-NULL and points to at least `N` elements, enabling additional optimizations.
Incorrect. Modifier `static` inside square brackets of parameter does not change storage class of array.
Incorrect. Syntax is official starting from C99 standard.
Incorrect. Array can contain *more* than 5 elements, but not fewer.

questions.topic: Variadic Functions — Automatic Type Promotions (Integer Promotions)
questions.q: To which data type are arguments of `char` and `short` types automatically promoted when passed to a function with unspecified number of arguments (`...`)?
questions.hint: Recall Default Argument Promotion rules for integer types smaller than int.
options: int (or unsigned int)
Types char and short are passed unchanged
long
double
explanations: Correct! When passing arguments to variadic functions, integer types smaller than `int` (such as `char` and `short`) are automatically promoted to `int` (or `unsigned int`). They must be extracted via `va_arg(args, int)`.
Incorrect. Type promotion always occurs when calling variadic functions.
Incorrect. Types `char` and `short` are not promoted to `long` by default.
Incorrect. `float` type is promoted to `double`, but not integer types.

questions.topic: Pointers to Arrays — Difference Between int* and int(*)[10]
questions.q: What does parameter `int (*arr)[10]` accept in function header?
questions.hint: Note parentheses around (*arr). This is a pointer to one single whole array.
options: Pointer to whole array of 10 elements of int type
Array of 10 pointers to int (int *arr[10])
Pointer to function returning array
Syntax error
explanations: Correct! Parentheses `(*arr)` set precedence: `arr` is pointer to fixed array of 10 elements of `int` type. Pointer step `arr + 1` equals $10 \times \text{sizeof(int)}$ bytes.
Incorrect. Entry without parentheses `int *arr[10]` declares array of 10 pointers.
Incorrect. Function pointer syntax includes argument parentheses: `int (*func)(int)`.
Incorrect. This is completely valid C syntax.

questions.topic: Function Prototypes — Omitting Parameter Names
questions.q: Is specifying only parameter types while omitting parameter names allowed in C function prototype (declaration) (e.g., `void log_msg(int, const char *);`)?
questions.hint: Does compiler need parameter names to check call signature?
options: Yes, parameter names in function prototypes are optional
No, names of all parameters must be specified in prototype
Allowed to omit name only for last parameter
explanations: Correct! For compiler in function prototype only data types and their order matter. Parameter names in declaration serve only for readability and can be omitted.
Incorrect. Requirement to specify parameter names exists only in function body definition.
Incorrect. Rule applies to any parameters in prototype.

questions.topic: Data Types — Passing Enumerations (enum)
questions.q: How are `enum` type values passed to C functions?
questions.hint: By which base type are enum constants represented in memory?
options: By value as integer values
Exclusively by pointer
As text strings with constant names
Enums are forbidden to pass into functions
explanations: Correct! In C, `enum` elements represent integer constants (usually of `int` type). Passing occurs by value via standard number copying.
Incorrect. Enumerations are scalar types and do not require passing by pointer.
Incorrect. Enum constant names exist only at compile stage and are not preserved as strings.
Incorrect. Enumerations are full-fledged C data type.

questions.topic: restrict Qualifier (C99) — Pointers Without Memory Overlap
questions.q: What do `restrict` qualifiers in pointer parameters of function `copy_data(int * restrict dst, const int * restrict src, int n)` inform compiler about?
questions.hint: Can pointers dst and src point to same or overlapping memory?
options: Pointed memory areas do not overlap, allowing compiler to perform aggressive vector optimizations
Pointers are constant and their addresses cannot change inside function
Function must execute strictly in single-threaded mode
Pointers are guaranteed non-NULL
explanations: Correct! `restrict` qualifier from C99 promises compiler that access to object during pointer lifetime will occur *only* through given pointer. This prevents aliasing (memory overlap) and gives optimizer freedom of action.
Incorrect. Constness of pointer itself is set by `int * const`.
Incorrect. Thread parallelism is not directly linked to `restrict` qualifier.
Incorrect. `restrict` qualifier does not perform NULL checks.

questions.topic: Passing Parameters — Modifying Pointer Copy
questions.q: What will `printf("%d", *ptr)` output after calling `shift(ptr)`?
questions.hint: Is pointer itself (variable ptr) passed by value to function shift?
options: Compilation error
explanations: Correct! Pointer `ptr` is passed to `shift` by value. Inside function local pointer copy `p++` is incremented. Original pointer `ptr` in `main` does not change its value and still points to 10.
Incorrect. Shifting pointer `ptr` itself in `main` would require passing `shift(&ptr)`.
Incorrect. Memory was not zeroed.
Incorrect. Code is written without errors.

questions.topic: C99 Syntax — Variable Length Arrays (VLA) in Parameters
questions.q: Which rule strictly regulates parameter order when passing Variable Length Array (VLA) into a function?
questions.hint: Can parameter n be used in brackets [n] if compiler has not encountered it in argument list yet?
options: Parameter n specifying array size must be located in parameter list STRICTLY BEFORE array parameter arr[n]
Parameter order does not matter
Parameter n must be specified strictly after array arr[n]
VLA arrays are forbidden to pass into functions
explanations: Correct! Compiler reads function header left to right. For expression `arr[n]` to compile, variable `n` must be declared above (to the left) in parameter list.
Incorrect. Order is strictly fixed left to right.
Incorrect. In that case `n undeclared` error will occur when parsing brackets `arr[n]`.
Incorrect. Passing VLA arrays is fully supported by C99 standard.

questions.topic: Passing Structures — Prohibition of Bit-field Addressing
questions.q: What will happen when attempting to pass an individual bit-field of a structure by pointer (calling `check(&h.flag)`)?
questions.hint: Does an individual bit-field (e.g., 1 bit in size) have its own unique address in memory?
options: Compilation error — taking address of a bit-field is directly forbidden by C standard
Code will compile successfully and pass address of byte containing field
Only NULL pointer will be passed
Bit-field will automatically copy to heap
explanations: Correct! Addressing in C works at byte level. Bit-fields may share a single byte and do not have their own unique address, so operator `&` applied to a bit-field is forbidden and causes compilation error.
Incorrect. Pointers reference byte address, not individual bit, so such call will not compile.
Incorrect. Error occurs at compile stage.
Incorrect. No memory allocation on heap occurs.
